analysis.one_liner: Restricts predatory online small-dollar lending, unauthorized account debits, and overdraft fees on prepaid cards.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 cosponsors, all Democrats, in February 2025; the Senate Banking Committee has taken no action on it since it was referred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds protections for people who borrow small amounts of money online or use prepaid debit cards. It would require small-dollar lenders to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, make online loans follow the interest-rate and fee rules of the borrower's home state (closing loopholes lenders use to dodge state caps), block checks and electronic debits that a borrower never authorized, give borrowers the right to stop automatic repayments, ban overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, and stop companies from collecting and selling people's bank account numbers to funnel them into payday-style loans. It also orders a government study of small-dollar lending on tribal lands.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who take out small-dollar loans online and prepaid card users. They would gain the right to stop automatic electronic repayments, protection from checks and debits they never authorized, their home state's interest-rate protections no matter where the lender is chartered, and an end to overdraft fees on prepaid accounts. People whose bank account details are currently bought and sold by lead-generation companies would also be protected.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small-dollar borrowers and prepaid card users

how_it_helps.text: Requires anyone making or brokering small-dollar loans ($5,000 or less, or a lower Bureau-set amount) to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before issuing credit. [S3]

Makes small-dollar loans made online, by phone, or by mail — and loans made by national banks — comply with the annual-percentage-rate, interest, and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, closing the loophole lenders use to export rates from a friendly state or charter. [S3]

Lets a remotely created check (a check not signed by the account owner) be issued only by a person the consumer designated in writing, revocable at any time, and bars payment orders issued in retaliation for a consumer exercising consumer-protection rights. [S3]
Treats a borrower's agreement to repay a small-dollar loan by electronic fund transfer as a preauthorized transfer, giving the borrower the law's existing stop-payment protections. [S3]
Prohibits overdraft fees on prepaid accounts and lets the Bureau bar other prepaid fees by rule. [S3]

Bars anyone who is not the actual lender from brokering or gathering applications involving sensitive financial data — Social Security numbers, bank account and routing numbers — in small-dollar lending, and requires such brokers to disclose who they are. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Online payday and installment lenders, companies that broker or buy loan applications and borrower data (lead generators), banks that rent out their charters so online lenders can evade state rate caps, and prepaid card issuers that charge overdraft fees. Some of these costs could be passed on as tighter lending standards or reduced credit availability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, lead generators, prepaid card issuers

drawbacks.text: Applying each state's rate caps to online and national-bank small-dollar loans could push some lenders out of the market in high-cap states, leaving borrowers who cannot qualify for bank credit with fewer options — the strongest good-faith objection to this kind of bill. [S3]
Registration and state-by-state compliance add costs to small-dollar lenders; some of that burden may fall on borrowers through reduced availability or changed loan terms. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target well-documented harms — unauthorized debits, loans structured to dodge state rate caps, overdraft fees on the poorest card users, and the sale of bank account data. The real tradeoff is credit availability: borrowers who rely on high-cost small-dollar loans and can't get bank credit could see fewer options if lenders exit strict states. On balance the bill shifts risk from borrowers to lenders, which is the design's stated purpose.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee on February 27, 2025, and the committee has not acted on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on February 27, 2025, joined by nine other Senate Democrats and one Independent. [S3]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day. [S5]
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything concrete because the bill has not moved. To the extent it stays buried, online small-dollar lenders, lead generators, and rent-a-bank arrangements benefit from the status quo, while borrowers continue to face unauthorized debits, out-of-state rates, and prepaid overdraft fees.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 27, 2025 and has taken no recorded action — no hearing or markup — since.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters are Democrats or Democratic-aligned Independents; no Republican senators have cosponsored, and the bill sits in a committee not acting on it.

industries.note: They would have to register with the CFPB and follow the borrower's home-state rate and fee laws, which would end the practice of chartering or locating in states with no rate caps. Their revenue depends on rates and fees many states do not permit.

The bill bars anyone who is not the actual lender from collecting and distributing borrowers' Social Security and bank account numbers in small-dollar lending, cutting off their business model of selling sensitive data to funnel consumers to lenders.

industries.industry: Banks that originate loans for online lenders (rent-a-bank arrangements)
industries.note: Loans made by national banks would have to comply with the borrower's home-state rate laws, removing the main way online lenders evade state interest-rate caps.
Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts — charged disproportionately to low-income users — would be banned, and the CFPB could bar other prepaid fees by rule.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action months after introduction, the bill's realistic path is to sit in the Banking Committee for the rest of the Congress unless it gains bipartisan support or a hearing. Similar Merkley lending bills in prior Congresses did not advance.
